content: Prolonging the survival of kidney transplants is a critical clinical goal. Induction immunosuppression using antibody therapy is a standard practice at the time of transplantation. Non-depleting interleukin-2 receptor monoclonal antibodies (IL2Ra) are considered the first-line agents for this purpose. For recipients at high risk of rejection, lymphocyte-depleting antibodies are often recommended, but the comparative benefits and risks of these agents remain unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate the relative and absolute effects of various antibody preparations (excluding IL2Ra) used for induction therapy in kidney transplant recipients. The study also aimed to assess how the benefits and adverse effects differ among antibody preparations, their formulations, and specific subgroups of recipients, such as children or sensitized individuals. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register up to August 29, 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies with placebo, no treatment, or other antibody therapies in adult and pediatric kidney transplant recipients were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two authors. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR), and continuous outcomes were reported as mean difference (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The review included 99 studies involving 8,956 participants, with 33 studies evaluating contemporary agents. Methodological reporting was incomplete in most studies, reducing confidence in the treatment effect estimates. Antithymocyte globulin (ATG) was found to reduce the risk of acute graft rejection (17 studies: RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.78). This benefit was consistent whether ATG was used with calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) therapy (12 studies: RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.76) or without it (5 studies: RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.98). However, the effects of ATG on mortality and graft loss were uncertain. For example, with CNI therapy, ATG showed uncertain effects on death at 3 to 6 months (3 studies: RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.22), 1 to 2 years (5 studies: RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.27 to 2.06), and 5 years (2 studies: RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.11 to 7.81). Similarly, its effects on graft loss were uncertain at 3 to 6 months (4 studies: RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.05) and 1 to 2 years (3 studies: RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.19). In non-CNI studies, ATG reduced death-censored graft loss (6 studies: RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.78) but had uncertain effects on mortality. When combining CNI and older non-CNI studies, ATG demonstrated a benefit at 1 to 2 years for all-cause graft loss (7 studies: RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.95) and death-censored graft loss (8 studies: RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.77), but these benefits were not sustained in the long term. ATG was associated with an increased risk of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (6 studies: RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.24 to 1.95), leucopenia (4 studies: RR 3.86, 95% CI 2.79 to 5.34), and thrombocytopenia (4 studies: RR 2.41, 95% CI 1.61 to 3.61). Its effects on delayed graft function, malignancy, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), and new-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT) were uncertain. Alemtuzumab was compared to ATG in six studies involving 446 patients, with early steroid withdrawal (ESW) or steroid minimization protocols. Alemtuzumab combined with steroid minimization reduced the risk of acute rejection at one year compared to ATG (4 studies: RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93). However, in two studies where ESW was only applied in the alemtuzumab arm, the effect on acute rejection at one year was uncertain (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.50 to 3.19). Alemtuzumab had uncertain effects on mortality at one year (2 studies: RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.06 to 2.42) and 2 to 3 years (3 studies: RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.15 to 2.95). Its effects on graft loss and death-censored graft loss were also uncertain. Creatinine clearance was lower with alemtuzumab plus ESW at six months (2 studies: MD -13.35 mL/min, 95% CI -23.91 to -2.80) and two years (2 studies: MD -12.86 mL/min, 95% CI -23.73 to -2.00) compared to ATG plus triple maintenance therapy. Across all six studies, the effects of alemtuzumab versus ATG on all-cause infection, CMV infection, BK virus infection, malignancy, and PTLD were uncertain. The impact of alemtuzumab with steroid minimization on NODAT was also unclear compared to ATG with steroid maintenance. Alemtuzumab combined with ESW, compared to triple maintenance without induction therapy, had uncertain effects on mortality, all-cause graft loss at one year, and acute rejection at six months and one year. However, CMV infection was increased (2 studies: RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.18 to 4.40). The effects on NODAT, thrombocytopenia, malignancy, and PTLD were poorly documented. Rituximab had uncertain effects on mortality, graft loss, acute rejection, and other adverse outcomes compared to placebo. In conclusion, ATG reduces the risk of acute rejection but has uncertain effects on mortality, graft survival, malignancy, and NODAT. It increases the risk of CMV infection, thrombocytopenia, and leucopenia. For every seven patients treated with ATG, one case of acute rejection is prevented, but one additional case of CMV disease occurs for every 12 patients treated. In the context of steroid minimization, alemtuzumab reduces acute rejection at one year compared to ATG, with 11 patients needing treatment to prevent one case of rejection. However, alemtuzumab increases the risk of CMV disease, with one additional case occurring for every six patients treated, without clear evidence of clinical benefit. Overall, while both ATG and alemtuzumab reduce acute rejection, they are associated with increased CMV disease, and neither appears to improve patient-centered outcomes such as reduced mortality or lower toxicity.
